title: Breathless lying flat a year after a heart attack
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 69-year-old woman brought to a metropolitan ED with 4 months of worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and ankle swelling a year after an anterior STEMI. The candidate then interprets her observations, ECG, bloods and chest X-ray, diagnoses decompensated biventricular heart failure, and outlines management and safety netting.
focus: Progressive breathlessness: quantifying exercise tolerance, eliciting left and right heart failure symptoms and risk factors, excluding the differentials, and starting heart failure management
stem: You are an intern in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Sophia Greenwood, a 69-year-old woman, has come in by ambulance complaining of shortness of breath. She is in an acute bay on a cardiac monitor with an IV cannula in place. A nurse is with you and can carry out your instructions. The nurse has taken her observations, recorded an ECG, sent bloods and requested a chest X-ray.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sophia and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you her observations, ECG, blood results and chest X-ray report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sophia Greenwood, a 69-year-old retired receptionist. You are sitting propped up on the trolley, a little breathless, and you speak in sentences but pause for breath now and then. You are worried and keep wondering whether this is your heart. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (when the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Sophia came in by ambulance about 20 minutes ago. At triage her resp rate was 26, sats 93% on room air, heart rate 104 and regular, BP 148/86, temperature 36.7, no pain. She slid down the trolley a few minutes ago and got more breathless lying back: on the repeat set her resp rate was 28, sats 92%, heart rate 108, BP 144/84. The ECG is done, the cannula is in, bloods have gone and the chest X-ray is requested."

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • If they sit you right up, you feel a little easier. If they lie you flat to examine you, you become more breathless and ask to sit up again.
  • If they ask the nurse to give oxygen, your sats rise to 96%.
  • If they ask the nurse to give a diuretic ("fluid tablet" or injection), the nurse asks: "What dose and route would you like?" If they give a dose and route, the nurse draws it up and gives it now, and you say you will probably need the toilet soon. If no dose is given, the nurse says she will wait for the dose before giving it. (Examiner: credit the dose element of item 36 only if the dose, 20 to 40 mg IV, is stated; the monitoring element can be earned in Part 2.)
  • If they ask for results in Part 1, the examiner says these will be given in Part 2.
  • If they use jargon, ask what it means.

Opening line: "Doctor, I am feeling very short of breath."

History (give only when asked):

The breathlessness

  • Onset: came on gradually about 4 months ago and has been slowly getting worse.
  • Worse with: exertion, and lying flat.
  • Better with: resting, and sleeping on more pillows.
  • How far you can walk: about 50 metres before you have to stop. Before this started you could walk about 500 metres easily. You now have to stop and rest while doing the grocery shopping.
  • Pillows: you now need 2 extra pillows to sleep.
  • At night: you wake up gasping for breath and have to sit on the edge of the bed until it settles. Last night was the worst so far, so your husband called the ambulance this morning.
  • Impact: "I can't do my daily activities properly because I feel so short of breath."

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Ankles: both ankles have been swollen for a few months, worse by the evening. Your socks leave deep marks.
  • No chest pain, no crushing or heavy feeling, nothing going to your arm, neck or jaw. No nausea or sweating.
  • No palpitations, no dizziness, no fainting.
  • No cough, no phlegm, no wheeze, no fever, sweats or shivers. No recent cold or flu.
  • No weight loss, your appetite is normal, no coughing up blood, no hoarse voice. No unusual tiredness apart from being puffed.
  • No tummy pain or swelling, no nausea or vomiting.
  • No calf pain. No feeling hot or cold all the time and no tremor.

Past medical history

  • Type 2 diabetes for 8 years.
  • High blood pressure for 15 years.
  • A heart attack 1 year ago. You were admitted to hospital and had a procedure to open the artery with a stent.
  • Osteoporosis.
  • Your immunisations are up to date.
  • Only if asked: you have never been told you have a heart murmur, an irregular heartbeat or a thyroid problem. No asthma or lung disease. No cancer and no chemotherapy.

Medications (you do not remember the doses)

  • Metformin for diabetes.
  • Perindopril and amlodipine for blood pressure.
  • Aspirin every day.
  • Denosumab injection every 6 months for your bones.
  • A multivitamin.
  • Nothing else. No fluid tablets.

Allergies: none.

Family history

  • Your father died of a heart attack at 52.
  • Your mother is 89 and has type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.
  • Your sister is 65, has type 2 diabetes and had a heart attack 1 year ago.
  • Your children are well.

Social history

  • Retired receptionist. You live with your husband; your children visit often and you have good support.
  • Smoking: ex-smoker. 15 cigarettes a day for 40 years; you quit 5 years ago.
  • Alcohol: 1 glass of wine a day.
  • Activity: you used to walk for 30 minutes every day, but now you can't.
  • Diet: you eat out and have takeaway often.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you wonder whether this is your heart, and you are frightened of having another heart attack like your father and sister. You want to be able to breathe easily and get back to your walks and your daily jobs.

Ask these during the history, once each, when there is a natural pause: "Could this be something to do with my heart?" and "Would I get another heart attack?"

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: sitting upright, propped on pillows, mildly breathless at rest, speaking in sentences. Not cyanosed, not pale, not sweaty. Overweight (84 kg).
  • Vital signs: as the nurse reported.
  • Hands and peripheries: warm, capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing, no tar staining, no tremor.
  • Pulse: 108/min, regular, normal volume.
  • Blood pressure: 144/84.
  • JVP: raised, 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, with a positive hepatojugular reflux.
  • Praecordium: apex beat displaced to the 6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. No heave or thrill.
  • Heart sounds: dual heart sounds with a third heart sound (gallop rhythm). No murmurs. No rub.
  • Respiratory: trachea central. Expansion equal. Dull to percussion at both bases. Fine inspiratory crackles at both bases to the lower third of the chest, with reduced breath sounds at the bases. No wheeze. No bronchial breathing.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Smooth liver edge palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. No ascites.
  • Legs and sacrum: bilateral pitting oedema to the mid-shins, symmetrical. Mild sacral oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.
  • Neck: no goitre, no lymphadenopathy.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Sophia's identity and asks whether she is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Recognises she is breathless: keeps questions short and focused, uses plain language and acknowledges her worry about her heart.
History
Characterises the breathlessness:
check.d: Credit when at least 3 of the 4 parts are covered, including quantified exercise tolerance against her baseline.

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over 4 months, slowly worsening, worst last night
Quantifies exercise tolerance against baseline: 50 m now, 500 m before; has to rest while grocery shopping
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse on exertion and lying flat; better with rest and extra pillows
Impact on function: cannot do daily activities, has stopped her daily 30-minute walk

check.x: Asks about left heart failure symptoms: orthopnoea (quantified as 2 extra pillows) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (wakes gasping, sits on the edge of the bed).
Asks about right heart failure symptoms: ankle swelling (both ankles, worse by evening) and abdominal swelling, right upper abdominal pain, nausea or poor appetite (absent).
check.d: Credit ankle swelling plus at least one abdominal or hepatic congestion symptom.

check.x: Asks about features of ischaemia and arrhythmia: central crushing chest pain, radiation, nausea, sweating, palpitations, dizziness and syncope (all absent).
Screens for respiratory differentials: cough, sputum, wheeze, fever and recent infection (COPD, asthma, pneumonia), all absent.
Screens for malignancy and systemic illness: weight loss, appetite, fatigue, haemoptysis, hoarseness and sweats (all absent).
Takes the past medical history: STEMI 1 year ago with PCI, type 2 diabetes for 8 years, hypertension for 15 years, osteoporosis.
check.d: Credit STEMI with PCI, type 2 diabetes and hypertension; osteoporosis not required.

check.x: Asks about other causes and risk factors for heart failure: known valve disease or murmur, arrhythmia, thyroid disease and chemotherapy (all absent).
check.d: Credit when at least 3 of the 4 are asked (valve disease/murmur, arrhythmia, thyroid, chemotherapy).

check.x: Takes a full medication history: metformin, perindopril, amlodipine, daily aspirin, 6-monthly denosumab and a multivitamin; no diuretic.
check.d: Credit the cardiovascular and diabetes medicines (perindopril, amlodipine, aspirin, metformin) and confirming no diuretic.

check.x: Asks about allergies (nil) and immunisations (up to date).
Takes a family history: father died of a heart attack at 52 (premature coronary disease), mother has diabetes and hypertension, sister has diabetes and had a heart attack a year ago.
Takes a social history:
check.d: Credit when at least 2 of the 3 are covered, including quantified smoking.

kids.x: Smoking quantified: 15 a day for 40 years (30 pack-years), quit 5 years ago
Alcohol (1 glass of wine a day) and diet (frequent takeaway and eating out, a salt load)
Home and support: lives with her husband, good family support; previous daily walks

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders if it is her heart, fears another heart attack, wants to get back to her daily activities. Acknowledges her questions and says they will be answered once the tests are back.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: sitting upright, work of breathing, speech in sentences, cyanosis, and the nurse's observations (RR 26 to 28, SpO2 93 to 92% on room air, HR 104 to 108).
Peripheral cardiovascular examination: pulse rate and rhythm (regular), BP, warmth and capillary refill (perfused), clubbing.
Assesses the JVP and finds it raised at 5 cm with a positive hepatojugular reflux.
Examines the praecordium: displaced apex beat, third heart sound (gallop), and listens for murmurs (no murmur heard; valve disease still to be assessed on echo).
Respiratory examination: bibasal fine inspiratory crackles, dullness and reduced breath sounds at both bases (effusions), no wheeze or bronchial breathing.
Examines for systemic venous congestion: bilateral symmetrical pitting oedema to the mid-shins, sacral oedema and smooth, non-tender hepatomegaly; calves non-tender.
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone and worse lying back, needing clinical review now; HR and BP in the white zone, afebrile, warm and perfused, so not shocked.
check.d: Credit yellow RR and SpO2, worse lying back, and not shocked (normal BP, perfused).

check.x: Interprets the ECG as sinus tachycardia with pathological Q waves in V1 to V4 and T inversion in V2 to V4 from the old anterior infarct, unchanged from the post-PCI ECG, with no new ischaemic ST change and no AF.
check.d: Credit sinus tachycardia, old anterior Q waves, unchanged from the previous ECG with no new ischaemic change.

check.x: Interprets the chest X-ray as cardiomegaly with upper lobe venous diversion, interstitial oedema with Kerley B lines and small to moderate bilateral effusions, with no consolidation, mass or hyperinflation.
check.d: Credit cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema or venous congestion and bilateral effusions, with no consolidation.

check.x: States that the markedly raised NT-proBNP (4850 ng/L) strongly supports heart failure.

States that the hs-troponin is mildly raised but flat (24 then 25 ng/L), so far most in keeping with chronic myocardial injury from heart failure, but the 0/1-h values are in the observe zone, so acute MI is not yet excluded and a further troponin (about 3 h) per the local pathway is needed.
check.d: Credit raised but flat troponin, likely chronic injury, AND that a further troponin is needed before MI is excluded.

check.x: Interprets the other bloods: mild hyponatraemia and creatinine above baseline (98 vs 84) as the pre-diuretic baseline; normal Hb and TSH, so anaemia and thyroid disease are not the cause.

Gives the diagnosis as decompensated biventricular heart failure, most likely ischaemic cardiomyopathy after her anterior STEMI. Justifies it with left-sided features (exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, crackles) and right-sided features (raised JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly), plus the results.
Gives at least 3 differentials, each with a feature against it: acute coronary syndrome, COPD, pneumonia, lung cancer, valvular heart disease.
Management

Escalates to the senior ED doctor or medical registrar, keeps her sitting upright (does not lie her flat) with continuous monitoring, titrates oxygen to SpO2 92 to 96% (TSANZ) (credit starting low-flow oxygen now for SpO2 92% falling with distress, or stating she will start it if SpO2 falls below 92%; no high-flow oxygen aimed above 96%), and admits her under medicine or cardiology.
check.d: Critical: credit when at least 3 of the 4 elements are covered, including senior escalation and the oxygen target (SpO2 92 to 96%).

check.x: Gives an IV loop diuretic at a correct dose: furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV for a diuretic-naive patient (40 mg reasonable here given her congestion and eGFR 52), reassesses breathing and urine output, with a fluid balance chart, daily weights and daily UEC with K and Mg.
check.d: Credit furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV (dose and route stated, in Part 1 or Part 2) plus at least two of: reassess breathing or urine output, fluid balance chart, daily weights, daily UEC with K and Mg.

check.x: States the escalation if she deteriorates: GTN if systolic BP is above 100 mmHg, and CPAP or NIV if she worsens.
Requests a transthoracic echocardiogram to measure LVEF and assess valves and wall motion, because the ejection fraction decides long-term treatment.

Reviews her medicines (considers stopping amlodipine, reviews metformin for her eGFR, prescribes VTE prophylaxis), starts a high-intensity statin now for secondary prevention, and once the echo is done and she is stable, plans HFrEF therapy (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARNI, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor).
check.d: Credit as a single item: at least one medication review step, starting the statin now (not deferred to the echo), and naming the four HFrEF classes.

check.x: Answers her questions in plain words: the heart pump has been weakened since the heart attack so fluid backs up into the lungs and legs; the tests so far do not show a new heart attack, and one more blood test later today will confirm this; medicines and lifestyle changes lower the risk of another one. Checks understanding.
Safety netting
Tells Sophia in plain words to tell the nurse at once in hospital, or call 000 after discharge, for chest pain, severe or sudden worsening breathlessness, fainting or a racing or irregular heartbeat.

Teaches daily morning weights (see the GP if up more than 2 kg in 2 days, more swelling or more pillows) and arranges GP review within about a week with repeat UEC, plus heart failure program, cardiology review and cardiac rehab.

part2.lead: Here are her observations, the ECG the nurse recorded, her blood results and the chest X-ray report. These results are now back, around 15:05 (repeat hs-troponin collected at 14:55). The observations shown are the two sets taken before your review.
part2.patient:
After the examiner reads question 4, ask these one at a time:

  • "Is it my heart, doctor?"
  • "Am I going to have another heart attack, like my dad?"

You are relieved if told the tests so far do not show a new heart attack. If the candidate explains clearly and kindly, you accept being admitted and ask them to tell your husband. If they use jargon, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Both sets taken on room air before medical review; the 13:58 set after she slid down the trolley and lay back.
handover.model:
• Read: at triage RR 26 and SpO2 93% on room air are in the yellow zone; HR 104, BP 148/86 and temperature 36.7 °C are white; no pain. At 13:58, lying back, RR 28 and SpO2 92% are still yellow and slightly worse, HR 108 (white), BP 144/84 (white).
  • Meaning: tachypnoea and borderline hypoxia that worsen lying back (orthopnoea), with a normal BP, warm peripheries and no fever: congestion without shock or sepsis.
  • Changes: the yellow zone calls for a clinical review, here a senior review now. Sit her up, titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 96% (start now or if it falls below 92%), and keep monitoring. A move into the red zone calls for a rapid response.

rows.note: Triage from ambulance: to acute bay, monitor on, ECG done
Repeat set: more breathless after slipping down flat on the trolley; sat up

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG of Mrs Sophia Greenwood, age 69, recorded at 13:50 today (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 104/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia. Regular, with a normal P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about -10°.
  • PR interval: 168 ms.
  • QRS duration: 104 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 452 ms (Bazett).
  • Q waves: pathological Q waves in V1 to V4 with poor R wave progression.
  • ST segments and T waves: ST segments isoelectric in all leads. Shallow T wave inversion in V2 to V4. No ST depression.
  • Other: no LVH by voltage criteria. No AF or flutter waves.
  • Comparison: ECG from discharge after PCI 12 months ago showed sinus rhythm at 72/min with the same Q waves in V1 to V4 and T inversion in V2 to V4. No new changes apart from the rate.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus tachycardia at 104/min, normal axis and intervals. Q waves V1 to V4 with poor R wave progression and shallow T inversion V2 to V4, unchanged from the post-PCI ECG. No new ST elevation or depression, no AF, no bundle branch block.
  • Meaning: an old anterior infarct (LAD territory), the likely substrate for an ischaemic cardiomyopathy. No new ischaemic changes, which is against ACS as the trigger. Sinus rhythm, so AF is not the precipitant.
  • Changes: HF is the working diagnosis; ACS is judged with the serial troponin. Repeat the ECG if chest pain or palpitations develop.

handover.label: Bloods
handover.model:
• Read: NT-proBNP 4850 ng/L, far above the acute HF rule-in level for her age. hs-troponin I 24 then 25 ng/L: above the women's 99th percentile of 16 but flat. Na 133 (mild hyponatraemia). Urea 9.6, creatinine 98 against a baseline of 84, eGFR 52. K and Mg normal. ALT 46 and bilirubin 23 mildly raised. Hb, WCC, TSH normal. Glucose 9.4, HbA1c 7.4%.
  • Meaning: heart failure confirmed biochemically. Stable low-level troponin is most in keeping with chronic myocardial injury from HF rather than an acute MI, pending the pathway's further troponin. Mild renal impairment and hyponatraemia fit congestion and reduced renal perfusion. LFTs show congestive hepatopathy. No anaemia, infection or thyroid cause; diabetes is above target.
  • Changes: the baseline electrolytes and renal function are needed before diuresis and HF medicines; recheck daily. Review metformin for her eGFR. An SGLT2 inhibitor would help both her HF and her diabetes. The 0/1-h values fall in the observe zone, so a further troponin per the local accelerated diagnostic pathway is required; the stable value with no chest pain and a 4-month course fits chronic injury.

rows.n: acute HF unlikely below 300; likely above 900 at age 50 to 75
target for most adults with diabetes 7.0 or below

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, AP erect (mobile), taken in the ED acute bay at 14:15.

Clinical details: 69-year-old woman with 4 months of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND and ankle oedema. Anterior STEMI with PCI 1 year ago. Ex-smoker, 30 pack-years. Bibasal crackles, raised JVP.

Findings:

  • Heart: enlarged, cardiothoracic ratio 0.62 (AP projection).
  • Pulmonary vessels: upper lobe venous diversion. Hila prominent and indistinct.
  • Lungs: bilateral interstitial opacities with peribronchial cuffing and Kerley B lines at both bases. No consolidation or air bronchograms. No mass or suspicious nodule. Lungs not hyperinflated.
  • Pleura: small to moderate bilateral pleural effusions, blunting both costophrenic angles with a meniscus at each base. No pneumothorax.
  • Mediastinum: not widened. Trachea central.
  • Bones and soft tissues: generalised osteopenia. No acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion, interstitial pulmonary oedema and small to moderate bilateral pleural effusions, in keeping with cardiac failure. No consolidation or mass.
handover.model:
• Read: an AP film magnifies the heart, but with a CTR of 0.62 and the other signs of congestion, cardiomegaly is likely; confirm on echo. Upper lobe diversion, interstitial oedema with peribronchial cuffing and Kerley B lines, small to moderate bilateral effusions. No consolidation, mass, hyperinflation or pneumothorax.
  • Meaning: congestive cardiac failure, matching the bibasal crackles and dull bases. No pneumonia; nothing to suggest lung cancer or COPD on this film.
  • Changes: supports diuresis now and an echo to measure LVEF. The effusions are bilateral and expected to clear with diuresis, so no tap is needed.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sophia Greenwood, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sophia now and over this admission.
Sophia has some questions about her heart. Please answer her questions, then explain to her the warning signs to look out for and tell me what follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED intern; Sophia Greenwood, 69.
  • Situation: decompensated biventricular heart failure; RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air before treatment (yellow, worse lying flat; give the current SpO2 and oxygen if started), HR 108, BP 144/84, afebrile.
  • Background: 4 months of exertional dyspnoea (50 m, was 500 m), 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling; anterior STEMI with PCI 1 year ago, T2DM, HTN, 30 pack-year ex-smoker; no diuretic, no statin.
  • Assessment: raised JVP 5 cm, S3, bibasal crackles and dull bases, oedema to mid-shins, non-tender hepatomegaly; RR and SpO2 in the yellow zone and worse lying back, but normotensive and warm, so not shocked. ECG: sinus tachycardia 104, old anterior Q waves V1 to V4, unchanged from the post-PCI ECG, no new ischaemia, no AF. CXR: cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, interstitial oedema, bilateral effusions, no consolidation. NT-proBNP 4850, strongly supports heart failure. hs-TnI 24 then 25 ng/L, raised but flat: most likely chronic myocardial injury from HF, but in the observe zone, so acute MI not yet excluded; 3-hour troponin due about 17:00. Na 133, creatinine 98 (baseline 84), Hb and TSH normal.
  • Recommendation: IV furosemide 20 to 40 mg (state if already given in Part 1); echo; please review and admit.

Decompensated biventricular heart failure, likely ischaemic cardiomyopathy after her anterior STEMI: left-sided (exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, crackles, CXR oedema) and right-sided (raised JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly) congestion; S3; NT-proBNP 4850; old anterior Q waves.

  • ACS (NSTEMI) as trigger: against: no chest pain, gradual course, flat troponin, unchanged ECG.
  • COPD: for: 30 pack-years; against: no cough, sputum or wheeze, no hyperinflation; spirometry once euvolaemic.
  • Pneumonia: against: afebrile, no cough, normal WCC, no consolidation.
  • Lung cancer: for: smoking, age; against: no weight loss, haemoptysis or hoarseness, no mass.
  • Valvular disease: against: no murmur; echo will confirm.

1. Senior review; sit upright; continuous monitoring; titrate oxygen to SpO2 92 to 96% (start now or if it falls below 92%); admit under medicine or cardiology.
  2. Furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV (diuretic-naive; 40 mg reasonable here), reassess breathing and urine output; fluid balance, daily weights, daily UEC with K and Mg.
  3. If she worsens: GTN if systolic BP is above 100 mmHg; CPAP or NIV.
  4. Transthoracic echo for LVEF.
  5. Consider stopping amlodipine; review metformin for eGFR; VTE prophylaxis.
  6. Start a high-intensity statin now for secondary prevention; once echo done and stable, HFrEF therapy (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARNI, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor).

• Plain words: yes, it is her heart. The heart attack weakened the pump, so fluid has built up in the lungs and legs. The tests so far do not show a new heart attack; one more blood test later today will confirm this. Medicines, diet and rehab lower the risk of another. Checks understanding.
  • Red flags (tell the nurse; 000 after discharge): chest pain, sudden or severe breathlessness, fainting, racing or irregular heartbeat.
  • See the GP promptly: weight up more than 2 kg in 2 days, more ankle swelling, needing more pillows.
  • Follow-up: daily morning weights; GP within about a week with repeat UEC; heart failure program, cardiology, cardiac rehab.

ddx.dx: Decompensated biventricular heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy after anterior STEMI
ddx.for: Four months of exertional dyspnoea, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling a year after an anterior STEMI, with a raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles, oedema, cardiomegaly and congestion on CXR and an NT-proBNP of 4850.

ddx.dx: Acute coronary syndrome (NSTEMI) precipitating heart failure
ddx.for: Previous STEMI, diabetes, hypertension, a premature family history and an hs-troponin above the 99th percentile.
ddx.against: No chest pain, a gradual 4-month course, a flat troponin (24 then 25) and an ECG unchanged from 12 months ago.

ddx.for: 30 pack-year ex-smoker with progressive exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: No cough, sputum or wheeze, orthopnoea and PND with oedema, and no hyperinflation on CXR.

ddx.for: Breathlessness with crackles at both bases.
ddx.against: Afebrile, no cough or sputum, normal WCC and no consolidation on CXR.

ddx.for: Age 69 with a 30 pack-year smoking history.
ddx.against: No weight loss, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no mass or nodule on CXR.

ddx.dx: Valvular heart disease (aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation)
ddx.for: Progressive exertional dyspnoea in an older woman with a dilated heart.
ddx.against: No murmur on examination; the echo will confirm.

guide:
In Part 1, the nurse gives the opening observations and Sophia answers the history. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. If the candidate lies her flat, she becomes more breathless and asks to sit up. If they ask for results in Part 1, say these will be given in Part 2. Credit treatment the candidate orders in Part 1 (sitting her up, oxygen, diuretic) against the Management items; credit the dose element of item 36 for a diuretic ordered in Part 1 only if the dose (20 to 40 mg IV) is stated; the monitoring element can be earned in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order. Sophia asks her questions after question 4 is read.

A high-performing candidate quantifies her exercise tolerance against her baseline. They elicit orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling, and link them to the STEMI a year ago. They screen quickly for ischaemia, arrhythmia, respiratory causes and malignancy. They examine the JVP, apex, heart sounds, lung bases, liver and legs. In Part 2 they read the old anterior Q waves as unchanged and the flat troponin as chronic injury, not a new MI. They diagnose biventricular failure from the CXR and NT-proBNP and give IV furosemide at a correct dose. They order an echo, plan the HF medicines by ejection fraction and answer her questions honestly in plain words.

A borderline candidate takes a generic breathlessness history without quantifying it and misses the PND or the previous heart attack. They do not examine the JVP or legs. They may call the raised troponin a new MI, or call the CXR "pneumonia" and give antibiotics. They may forget the echo or the electrolyte monitoring. Laying her flat, or giving no diuretic, is a safety concern.

If the candidate gave oxygen or furosemide in Part 1, accept a handover that reports them as given.
explain:
Diagnosis: decompensated biventricular heart failure

Sophia has heart failure with congestion on both sides of the circulation. The most likely cause is an ischaemic cardiomyopathy after her anterior STEMI a year ago. After an MI, loss of contracting muscle and ventricular remodelling dilate and weaken the left ventricle. Her hypertension, diabetes and smoking history add to the damage.

  • Left heart failure causes pulmonary venous congestion: exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, bibasal crackles and pulmonary oedema.
  • Right heart failure causes systemic venous congestion: raised JVP, peripheral and sacral oedema, and hepatomegaly. Liver congestion can cause right upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, and mildly abnormal liver tests.
  • Left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure.

Over the past 4 months, being breathless after 50 m (previously 500 m), i.e. on less than ordinary activity, put her in NYHA class III. Today she is breathless at rest, which is NYHA class IV while she is decompensated. Possible precipitants include a high-salt diet (frequent takeaway) and the absence of any heart failure treatment.

The history

Quantify breathlessness against the patient's baseline: distance, flights of stairs or named activities. Ask about orthopnoea (how many pillows) and PND, and about right-sided symptoms. Exclude the differentials:

  • Ischaemia: chest pain, radiation, nausea, sweating.
  • Arrhythmia: palpitations, dizziness.
  • Respiratory disease: cough, sputum, wheeze, fever.
  • Malignancy: weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness.

Then cover the heart failure risk factors: coronary disease and MI, age, diabetes, hypertension, family history, alcohol, smoking, arrhythmia, valve disease, infiltrative disease, chemotherapy and thyroid disease.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: RR and SpO2 are in the yellow zone and worsen lying back, which calls for clinical review. She is perfused and normotensive, so she is not in cardiogenic shock.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia with old anterior Q waves, unchanged from the earlier ECG. There is no new ischaemia and no AF.
  • Chest X-ray: a mobile AP film magnifies the heart, but a CTR of 0.62 with signs of congestion makes cardiomegaly likely (the echo confirms it). There is upper lobe diversion, interstitial oedema with Kerley B lines and small to moderate effusions.
  • NT-proBNP: a low value makes heart failure unlikely (below 300 ng/L in the acute setting). Hers is very high and strongly supports the diagnosis.
  • Troponin: hs-troponin is often mildly raised in heart failure. A stable value without a significant rise or fall is chronic myocardial injury. A rise or fall with a fitting clinical picture would point to an acute MI. Values in the observe zone of a 0/1-h pathway need a further troponin before MI is excluded.
  • Other bloods: hyponatraemia and a creatinine above baseline reflect congestion and reduced renal perfusion. Normal Hb and TSH exclude anaemia and thyroid disease as contributors.

Differentials

  • ACS triggering decompensation must be excluded with the ECG and serial troponin.
  • COPD is possible in a 30 pack-year ex-smoker. Spirometry is best done once she is euvolaemic.
  • Pneumonia and lung cancer are made unlikely by the history and the CXR.
  • Valve disease, especially aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation, is assessed on the echo.
  • Amlodipine can cause ankle swelling, but not orthopnoea, PND or a raised JVP.

Management (Heart Foundation and CSANZ heart failure guidelines; eTG Cardiovascular)

  1. Acute: sit her upright, monitor continuously and titrate oxygen to a target SpO2 of 92 to 96% (TSANZ): start it now, as her saturations are borderline and falling with distress, or as soon as SpO2 falls below 92%, and avoid high-flow oxygen aimed above 96%. Give IV furosemide, 20 to 40 mg if she is diuretic-naive (40 mg is reasonable here given her congestion); patients already on a loop diuretic need at least their usual oral dose IV. Repeat it according to her response. Monitor fluid balance, daily weights and daily electrolytes, renal function, potassium and magnesium, and consider fluid and salt restriction while she is congested. Give VTE prophylaxis. If she develops acute pulmonary oedema, give GTN (sublingual, then infusion) if systolic BP is above 100 mmHg, avoiding it if systolic BP is below 90 mmHg, and start CPAP or NIV for respiratory failure.
  2. Echocardiography: measures LVEF to classify heart failure as reduced or preserved ejection fraction, and assesses wall motion and the valves.
  3. HFrEF treatment once stable:
    • A beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate or nebivolol), started low once euvolaemic and titrated up.
    • An ACE inhibitor, or a switch to sacubitril/valsartan after a 36-hour ACE inhibitor washout.
    • A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, with potassium and renal monitoring.
    • An SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin), which also helps her diabetes.
    • Loop diuretics to control congestion.
  4. Other medicines: amlodipine has no heart failure benefit and causes oedema, so it can be stopped to make room for these medicines. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are avoided in HFrEF. Metformin is reviewed for her eGFR and withheld if she becomes hypoperfused or her renal function worsens.
  5. Secondary prevention after MI: aspirin and a high-intensity statin. Cardiology input on residual ischaemia.
  6. Multidisciplinary care: the heart failure nurse, pharmacist, dietitian and physiotherapist during the admission; a heart failure disease management program, cardiac rehabilitation and dietitian advice on salt and takeaway food. Keep alcohol low and keep vaccinations up to date.

Safety netting and follow-up

Sophia should call 000 for chest pain, sudden or severe breathlessness, fainting or a racing irregular heartbeat. She should weigh herself every morning and see her GP promptly if her weight rises by more than 2 kg over 2 days, her ankles swell more or she needs more pillows. Arrange a GP review within about a week of discharge with repeat electrolytes and renal function, enrolment in a heart failure program, cardiology review and cardiac rehabilitation.
points: Quantify breathlessness against the patient's baseline (distance, stairs or activities) and ask specifically about orthopnoea (number of pillows), PND and ankle swelling.

Left heart failure causes pulmonary congestion (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, crackles); right heart failure causes systemic congestion (raised JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly). Left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure.
A previous MI is a leading cause of heart failure through loss of contractility and remodelling. Check that patients after an MI are on secondary prevention, including a statin.

NT-proBNP supports or rules out heart failure. A mildly raised but stable hs-troponin is most often chronic myocardial injury; values in the observe zone of a 0/1-h pathway need a further troponin before MI is excluded, and acute MI needs a significant rise or fall with a fitting clinical picture.

Treat congestion with IV furosemide (20 to 40 mg if diuretic-naive), monitor weights, fluid balance and electrolytes, and get an echo because the LVEF decides long-term therapy (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor or ARNI, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor in HFrEF).
Teach daily weights: a gain of more than 2 kg over 2 days, worse swelling or more breathlessness means seeing the GP promptly; chest pain or severe breathlessness means calling 000.
